title: Memo Teleprinter
pitch: Type or paste any office memo and a clattering fictional teleprinter turns it into a five-voice rhythm: each letter's 5-bit teleprinter code lights five tracks, and buzzwords from a bundled jargon bank trigger absurd stabs and fanfares. A Euclid dial re-spaces the notes as evenly as possible and the 'cc' list cascades the memo down through ever more bureaucratic echoes. Every memo has its own groove; export the link and send your boss a tune.
whyNow: Timeless office-satire with a mechanic that is genuinely musical: five-bit character codes naturally map to five parallel gates, and Euclidean spacing turns gibberish into something that grooves.

research.summary: Teleprinter codes of the telegraph era used five bits per character, with two shift codes switching between letters and figures; that gives 32 patterns, a ready-made mapping from text to five parallel on/off tracks. Euclidean rhythms, described by Toussaint in 2005, distribute k onsets over n pulses as evenly as possible and reproduce dozens of traditional timelines, for example E(3,8) the tresillo; they come from an algorithm devised for timing neutron beams that mirrors Euclid's greatest-common-divisor method. Combining the two lets typed text drive rhythm and then be re-spaced by an Euclid control. The humour comes from invented, harmless office jargon and a mock-solemn teleprinter persona; no real company, person or brand is used.

sources.snippet: Baudot's telegraph code uses five bits per character, with shift codes between letters and figures; its descendant ITA2 was the standard teleprinter code until 7-bit ASCII.

facts.claim: Baudot-family teleprinter codes use five bits per character, with shift codes switching between letters and figures, so 32 patterns per shift; ITA2 descended from it and preceded 7-bit ASCII (1963).

Euclidean rhythms E(k,n) spread k onsets over n pulses as evenly as possible and are linked by Toussaint (2005) to Euclid's algorithm and to Bjorklund's accelerator-timing algorithm; E(3,8) is the tresillo.
Bjorklund's algorithm was devised for timing neutron beam pulses at a particle accelerator, per one search summary that blended several results; treated as unconfirmed here.

design.coreLoop: Write or paste a memo, press send, and watch the teleprinter print it character by character while five tracks fire from each letter's 5-bit code. Jargon words from a bundled bank trigger special stabs, and the Euclid dial and cc cascade reshape the same memo into new grooves. Trying different memos, subject lines and dial settings keeps revealing new rhythms and new jokes, and each result has a shareable link.
sophisticationHooks: Exact 5-bit letter and figure table with shift codes, so the figures-shift in a memo audibly changes the pattern
Euclidean re-spacing of each track from the memo's own letter counts, with seeded variation so the same memo always plays the same tune
Procedural WebAudio voices (clattering type bars, bell, carriage return, stabs) with no samples, plus a printed-paper canvas view that scrolls in sync
Bundled fictional jargon bank with invented company names, mapped to fanfares; URL hash stores memo text, dial and seed
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: 5-bit code table, text-to-pattern engine, five procedural voices, scheduler with swing, canvas paper and key-bed view, textarea with sample memos, Euclid dial, cc cascade echoes, share-hash, about panel. Cut: recording and export, multiple languages, user-supplied jargon banks.
risks: Humour needs good invented copy; mitigate with a writer-owned jargon bank and sample memos that are fictional only
Must avoid any real company, person or brand names; all sender names and firms are invented and labelled as parody
Bjorklund origin story is only from a blended search summary, so the about panel leaves it out or says reported, unconfirmed
